title: Design Moderators of Perceived Residential Crowding and Chronic Physiological Stress Among Children
research_question: This study aimed to (a) examine the association between residential interior density and children's perceived home and bedroom crowding, and (b) investigate whether interior design attributes (floor plan arrangement, bedroom ceiling height, volume, and window area) moderate the effects of perceived crowding on children's psychological health and chronic physiological stress.

participants.description: Children (mean age = 9 years) and their mothers from low- and middle-income families, primarily residing in rural areas throughout upstate New York. 88% White. 50% lived in detached, single-family homes.
participants.recruitment: Home interviews conducted during two home visits by trained research assistants as part of a larger longitudinal study (Wave 1, 1995-1999).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Children's actual home environments, characterized by measured interior density (persons per room) and specific design attributes of the home and the focus child's bedroom (FCB).

mechanisms: Perceived crowding arises from difficulties in regulating social interaction, diminished feelings of control, overarousal/overstimulation, or interference with goals and activities.
Higher ceiling heights may increase perceived personal space or overall room volume, thereby reducing perceived crowding and buffering its negative effects.
Children's ability to retreat to a private space (like a bedroom) and control social interactions may attenuate negative effects of high interior density and perceived crowding.
implementation_implications: Increasing residential ceiling heights, or adjusting other design attributes that affect perceptions of ceiling height, could buffer adverse effects of perceived crowding on residents, including children, especially when increasing square footage is not possible.
Designers should consider physical design features beyond available floor space to attenuate negative effects of high interior density associated with crowding.

limitations: The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inferences.
It did not account for length of exposure to high interior density, previous living conditions, parent behavior and well-being, noise, or other stressors.
The sample size was relatively small (N=181), and there was low variability among some study variables, which may have limited the detection of other significant effects.
The reliability of perceived crowding measures used with young children requires further testing.
Other potentially relevant design attributes (e.g., openness, visual access, acoustic treatments, lighting) were not examined.
Results regarding mean home depth were inconsistent with prior work, possibly due to the rural/small town setting and low-rise buildings in the sample.

paper_metadata.title: Design Moderators of Perceived Residential Crowding and Chronic Physiological Stress Among Children
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Design Moderators of Perceived Residential Crowding and Chronic Physiological Stress Among Children
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Chronic crowding within housing adversely affects psychological well-being, yet little is known about how design attributes contribute to these effects, especially among children. This cross-sectional study first examined associations between residential interior density and children’s ( M = 9 years of age) perceived bedroom and home crowding. Second, analyses investigated whether interior design attributes (residential floor plan arrangement measured by space syntax [depth and permeability]; bedroom ceiling height, volume, and window area) buffer negative effects of perceived crowding on multimethodological indices of child development, including psychological distress, learned helplessness, and physiological stress. After adjusting for home type, clutter, income, gender, and age, interior density was significantly associated with perceived home and bedroom crowding. Regression results suggested that bedroom ceiling height was associated with reduced negative effects of home, but not bedroom, perceived crowding on blood pressure, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and allostatic load among participants who reported higher levels of perceived crowding.
